name: Lambardi Tower of Magione
region: Province of Perugia, Umbria — Magione, eastern shore of Lake Trasimeno
address: Via della Torre, 06063 Magione PG, Italy
architectural_style: Knights Hospitaller medieval tower, 12th–13th century — built by the Knights of Jerusalem (Knights Hospitaller) on a forested hillside above Magione's historic centre; a compact cylindrical structure of rough-cut Central Italian stone with minimal later exterior modification; the interior has been fitted with a contemporary immersive projection museum circuit while preserving the historic medieval shell; the nearby Castle of the Knights of Malta is a companion Hospitaller monument in the same town, giving Magione an unusual concentration of surviving Hospitaller architecture in Umbria

opening_hours.seasonal_note: Open Tuesday–Sunday; closed Monday. Summer hours (June–September) may extend to 19:00 on weekends. Confirm current hours at the Comune di Magione or via the GYG ticket before visiting. Temporary exhibitions update 2–3 times annually; check the current programme before booking.

visit_duration: 45 minutes–1.5 hours (self-guided tower circuit with immersive projections, exterior terrace, and any current temporary exhibition)
best_season: April to June and September to October — Umbria is a year-round destination but spring and autumn are most comfortable for walking; the cypress and holm oak landscape around the tower is particularly atmospheric in October. July–August can be warm and the site has limited shade outside the tower.
accessibility: The path to the tower from Magione town centre involves a short uphill walk on a paved lane. The tower interior involves period stairs; no elevator. Not fully wheelchair accessible. The exterior terrace and lower level are accessible for most visitors.
tagline: The Umbrian tower where a Franciscan friar reached the Mongol court 25 years before Marco Polo — and a museum of immersive projections on medieval border-crossing
highlights: Giovanni da Pian del Carpine — Magione's pre-Marco-Polo traveller to the Mongol Empire — a Franciscan friar born in Magione around 1185, Giovanni undertook a papal diplomatic mission in 1245–1246 to the court of Great Khan Güyük in Karakorum, Mongolia; he returned to write the Historia Mongalorum, the first systematic European account of the Mongol Empire from direct observation — roughly 25 years before Marco Polo's more famous expedition

Knights of Jerusalem / Knights Hospitaller origins — the tower was constructed by the Knights Hospitaller between the 12th and 13th centuries as part of the order's territorial presence in Umbria; the nearby Castle of the Knights of Malta is a companion Hospitaller monument in the same town, making Magione an unusual concentration of surviving Hospitaller architecture in Central Italy

Immersive museum circuit on the Giovanni expedition and the tower's history — the interior hosts contemporary projection installations covering the tower's Hospitaller origins and Giovanni da Pian del Carpine's journey to Karakorum; rotating temporary exhibitions update 2–3 times annually, giving the visit a different character across the year

Lake Trasimeno views from the upper terrace — the view from the tower extends toward the fourth largest lake in Italy; the same lake shoreline was the site of Hannibal's ambush of the Roman consul Gaius Flaminius in 217 BCE, one of the most tactically decisive defeats in Roman military history

One of the most affordable heritage visits in Umbria — admission at approximately €3 is significantly below the average for comparable museum circuits in the region, and the site is rarely congested; a genuine hidden-gem alternative to the major Umbrian heritage destinations for visitors based in Perugia or at Lake Trasimeno
description:
The Torre dei Lambardi rises from a forested hillside above Magione, a small commune on the eastern shore of Lake Trasimeno. The lake — the fourth largest in Italy, set in a shallow bowl of hills between Umbria and Tuscany — gives this corner of central Italy a particular quality of light: blue and reflective in clear weather, grey and atmospheric when the mountains generate cloud. Most visitors who reach Lake Trasimeno concentrate on Castiglione del Lago to the west or take the ferry to Isola Maggiore. Magione, on the eastern bank, is quieter, and it retains more of the physical texture of a medieval Umbrian settlement.

The tower occupies a wooded promontory above the town centre, approached through holm oak and cypress — characteristically Umbrian landscape. The fortification was built by the Knights of Jerusalem, the military religious order also known as the Knights Hospitaller, during the 12th or early 13th century. The Hospitallers had a significant presence in this part of Umbria; the nearby Castle of the Knights of Malta is a companion monument from the same institution, and together the two structures give Magione an unusual concentration of surviving Hospitaller architecture in Central Italy. Both buildings stand as evidence of the order's territorial reach during the medieval period — the Hospitallers were simultaneously a military force, a religious community, and a major property-holding institution across Catholic Europe.

The connection that gives the Torre dei Lambardi its most unusual historical claim is not architectural but biographical. Magione was the birthplace, around 1185, of Giovanni da Pian del Carpine — a Franciscan friar who in 1245 undertook a diplomatic journey that no European of his era had attempted before and few have equalled since. Pope Innocent IV, alarmed by the Mongol invasions of Poland and Hungary in 1241 and uncertain about Mongol intentions toward Christian Europe, sent Giovanni eastward as a papal emissary. Giovanni was in his sixties, in poor health, and the journey he undertook was extraordinary even by medieval standards.

Travelling from Lyon through Poland and across the Eurasian steppe, spending more than a year on horseback, Giovanni reached the Mongol capital of Karakorum — in what is now central Mongolia — in time for the formal enthronement of the Great Khan Güyük in July 1246. He attended the ceremony, presented the Pope's letters, and received Güyük's reply — in effect a demand that the Pope and Christian rulers submit to Mongol authority. Giovanni returned to Europe and wrote the Historia Mongalorum, a systematic account of the Mongol Empire: its political structure, military methods, geography, religious practices, and the sheer territorial scale of the empire stretching from China to the borders of Hungary. The Historia is the earliest detailed European description of the Mongol Empire written from direct observation.

Marco Polo would not begin his journey until 1271 — roughly a quarter century after Giovanni had already returned from Karakorum and completed his written account. This sequence is not widely known outside specialist circles; Marco Polo's name and narrative have far eclipsed Giovanni's in cultural memory, though Giovanni's account preceded and in several respects surpassed the Venetian's in diplomatic precision and systematic intent. The museum circuit inside the Torre dei Lambardi addresses this directly. Immersive projection installations cover both the tower's medieval history as a Hospitaller fortification and Giovanni's eastern journey — the route across the Eurasian steppe, the Mongol court at Karakorum, the political context of the mid-13th century encounter between Latin Christendom and the Mongol Empire, and the figure of Giovanni himself.

The visit is self-guided and structured around the tower's interior rooms and the exterior terrace. The projections use period sources and contemporary cartography to trace the journey from the Umbrian hills where Giovanni was born to the Mongolian steppe where the Great Khan received him. Alongside the permanent installation, the tower hosts rotating temporary exhibitions; the programme changes two or three times annually, and the character of the visit shifts accordingly. Entry at approximately €3 is among the most affordable for any museum circuit of comparable historical reach in Umbria, and the site is rarely crowded — a genuine hidden-gem alternative to the major Umbrian heritage destinations.

From the tower's upper terrace, the view extends across Magione toward Lake Trasimeno. The lake is where, in 217 BCE, the Carthaginian general Hannibal ambushed and annihilated a Roman army under the consul Gaius Flaminius — one of the most tactically decisive defeats in Roman military history and one of Hannibal's most celebrated victories. Hannibal concealed his forces in the wooded hills above the lake shore and attacked the Roman column simultaneously from three sides as it passed below. The battle has no commemorative monument at Magione specifically, but the lake visible from the tower connects the contemporary visitor to an event that transformed the trajectory of the Second Punic War and, through it, the history of Rome.

Magione is approximately 25km from Perugia on the SS220, connected by regular regional bus services from Perugia's bus station. The town centre below the tower has small trattorias and a Saturday market. The tower is a short steep walk from the main piazza. The full circuit — travel from Perugia, the visit, and return — can be completed comfortably in a half day; visitors based in Perugia might combine the tower with a Lake Trasimeno circuit (ferry to Isola Maggiore, lunch at Castiglione del Lago) for a full day.

[Rocca Paolina](/castles/italy/rocca-paolina) — the vast subterranean papal fortress built by Pope Paul III beneath the streets of Perugia in the 1540s, its original medieval streets and buildings intact underground — is approximately 25km northwest of Magione. The Rocca Paolina is one of the most unusual fortress-museum experiences in Central Italy, its circuit running entirely below the city through the buried fabric of the medieval neighbourhood that was demolished to build the papal stronghold.
history: 12th–13th century: Knights Hospitaller (Knights of Jerusalem) construct the Torre dei Lambardi on a forested hillside above Magione as part of the order's territorial presence in Umbria; the nearby Castle of the Knights of Malta is built in the same period. c. 1185: Giovanni da Pian del Carpine born in Magione; he will later become a Franciscan friar and diplomat. 1245–1246: Giovanni travels on papal mission from Lyon to the Mongol capital of Karakorum, attending the enthronement of Great Khan Güyük; returns with the Historia Mongalorum, the first systematic European account of the Mongol Empire. Late medieval period: Magione and Lake Trasimeno absorbed into the Papal States. 16th century: Papal States consolidate control of Umbria; the tower loses its military function. 19th century: unification of Italy; Umbria incorporated into the Kingdom of Italy. 20th–21st century: the Torre dei Lambardi conserved by the Comune di Magione; converted into a museum circuit with immersive projection installations documenting the tower's Hospitaller history and Giovanni da Pian del Carpine's Mongol expedition. Present day: open to visitors Tuesday–Sunday; permanent immersive projection circuit plus rotating temporary exhibitions.
how_to_visit:
**GYG admission ticket (~$3.30/person, t1394566, valid 1 day):** Covers entrance to the full tower circuit including immersive projections and any current temporary exhibition. New activity — 0 reviews. Book via GYG to confirm current hours before visiting.

**Getting there:** Magione is approximately 25km southeast of Perugia on the SS220. By bus: regular regional services from Perugia bus station (APM Perugia) to Magione, approximately 40 minutes. By car: SS220 from Perugia (30 minutes); limited parking in Magione town centre. The tower is a short steep walk from Piazza Fratamaggiore. By train: Perugia Fontivegge to Magione is not served by a direct rail connection; bus is the practical option.

**Visiting in context:** Combine with a Lake Trasimeno day — ferry from San Feliciano to Isola Maggiore, lunch at Castiglione del Lago — for a full day from Perugia. The Rocca Paolina underground fortress in Perugia is the most directly comparable Umbrian fortress-museum experience.

faqs.question: Who was Giovanni da Pian del Carpine and why does the tower commemorate him?
faqs.answer: Giovanni da Pian del Carpine was a Franciscan friar born in Magione around 1185 who undertook a papal diplomatic mission to the Mongol Empire in 1245–1246 — roughly 25 years before Marco Polo's more famous journey. Pope Innocent IV sent him to the court of Great Khan Güyük in Karakorum (now central Mongolia), both to assess Mongol military intentions after the invasions of Poland and Hungary and to seek possible alliance against the Islamic powers of the Middle East. Giovanni travelled by horse across the Eurasian steppe, attended the enthronement of the Great Khan, received a reply letter (effectively demanding papal submission), and returned to write the Historia Mongalorum — the first systematic European account of the Mongol Empire. The tower's museum circuit documents his journey with immersive projections; his connection to Magione gives the site its most unusual historical claim.

faqs.question: What does the €3 admission ticket include?
faqs.answer: The GYG admission ticket (t1394566, approximately €3) covers the full self-guided visit to the Torre dei Lambardi: the immersive projection installations inside the tower rooms documenting the Hospitaller history of the building and Giovanni da Pian del Carpine's diplomatic mission to the Mongol Empire, access to the exterior terrace with views toward Lake Trasimeno, and entry to any current temporary exhibition. No guided tour is included in the standard ticket; the visit is self-paced with the projection programme providing the interpretive content.

faqs.question: Is the Lambardi Tower the same as the Castle of the Knights of Malta in Magione?
faqs.answer: No — they are separate structures. The Torre dei Lambardi and the Castello dei Cavalieri di Malta (Castle of the Knights of Malta) are both Hospitaller monuments in Magione, built by the same order, but they are distinct buildings with separate histories, separate access, and separate functions. The Tower hosts the Giovanni da Pian del Carpine museum circuit; the Castle is a larger fortified complex nearby. The GYG ticket (t1394566) covers the Tower specifically. Both can be seen on the same visit to Magione.
